extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology/social psychology of humour and emotion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and analysing sociological/psychological criteria that link embarrassment and humour: types of embarrassing situations, their social functions, developmental learning, observers' reactions, and remedial/disciplinary roles of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment as a lesser form of shame
rubrics_metrics.description: Scheff specifically identifies embarrassment as a lesser form of shame; embarrassment can be experienced intensely despite trivial provoking causes (e.g., calling someone by the wrong name, forgetting to zip clothing, spilling coffee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the disjunction between the triviality of the provocation and intensity of feeling; useful when diagnosing emotional responses in social incidents or when distinguishing shameful from merely embarrassing acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goffman’s mechanism: embarrassment enforces social codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Goffman explains that social actors routinely accept constraints because social embarrassment is built into social life, threatening actors with a form of social death each time they forget codes of appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to explain conformity and routine self-policing: the fear of embarrassment explains maintenance of social order without complex psychoanalytic accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three types of embarrassing situations (Sabini et al., 2000)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sabini et al. suggest three main types of embarrassing situations: faux pas (failure to negotiate routine interaction), sticky situations (things turning out wrongly, requiring actions that may discredit someone else), and being the centre of attention (distinct from the other two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify incidents into these three categories when analysing why an event is experienced as embarrassing; examples: wrong clothing = faux pas; ex-partner showing up = sticky situation; public attention = centre-of-attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goffman’s emphasis on tricky situations with conflicting expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Goffman concentrates on embarrassment arising from conflicts of expectations (e.g., managers encountering workers in egalitarian settings), where displays of fumbling and embarrassment contribute to maintenance of social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining institutional or hierarchical interactions, identify expectation conflicts and how embarrassed displays signal multiple social selves rather than breakdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour as face-saving/remedial strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Goffman (footnote) and later researchers argue joking/joshing can relieve tension in moments of expected equality (superior/junior) and that humour can perform face-saving work to deny the same reality embarrassment denies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider humour among participants as an explicit remedial strategy alongside apologies/excuses; humour can downgrade seriousness and help actors 'come through' tricky moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embarrassment is learned; developmental onset around age nine
rubrics_metrics.description: Infants do not show physiological signs of embarrassment (e.g., blushing); a sense of embarrassment develops with the social self and is learned through socialization and ridicule, with full-blown embarrassment emerging around age nine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this when analysing developmental acquisition of social emotions: early ridicule by older children teaches children both to feel embarrassment and that others may laugh at inappropriate behaviour (e.g., toilet-training contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Onlookers often find others' embarrassment funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment may be painful for the actor but frequently funny to onlookers; tricky situations and gaffes provide material for comedy because the audience enjoys the discomfort of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing comedic content or audience response, note that observed discomfort frequently produces laughter; example: theatrical/farce uses gaffes and awkwardness for humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of embarrassing situations (Miller): normative public deficiencies and temporary stupidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Miller classifies common embarrassing situations as 'normative public deficiencies' (bodily losses of control such as laughing/coughing/farting in public) and 'temporary stupidity' (cognitive errors like forgetting names or saying the wrong word).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these subtypes to categorize embarrassing incidents and predict likely audience reactions; examples include bodily eruptions in formal occasions or public verbal slips (George Bush quote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting condition for laughter: event must be embarrassing not shameful
rubrics_metrics.description: A limiting condition on laughter at others’ misfortunes is that the gaffe should not transgress deep moral codes—in other words, it should be embarrassing rather than shameful to provoke humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an incident is morally transgressive (eliciting shame) versus merely inappropriate (eliciting embarrassment) before predicting humour response; moral violations reduce comedic license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap between events that make people laugh and those that embarrass
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies (Van Giffen & Maher) show that events people recount as funny are very similar to events people report as embarrassing; many funny episodes are instances of normative public deficiencies or temporary stupidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When collecting humorous anecdotes or designing humour studies, expect substantial overlap with embarrassment vignettes (e.g., dessert falling into lap, neighbors crashing into wall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict between empathy and laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers may experience a conflict between empathy (displaying sympathy for the embarrassed actor) and the compulsion to laugh; the two responses cannot be enacted simultaneously (e.g., hurrying a laughing sister out of sight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysing audience or bystander reactions, consider situational constraints on simultaneous prosocial displays and mirth; note Bergsonian tension between empathy and laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Nice-guy’ theory vs enjoyment of watching embarrassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Social-science accounts often emphasize empathetic/onlooker remedial behaviour (the 'nice guy' view), but these accounts may overlook observers' malicious or vicarious enjoyment of others' embarrassment (e.g., popularity of I Love Lucy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of explanatory bias that privileges empathy; include the possibility of audience enjoyment or malicious pleasure as a legitimate reaction when analysing social laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial strategies used by embarrassed actors and onlookers
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial strategies in embarrassing situations include apologies, excuses, justifications and humour; both the embarrassed actor and onlookers may use these to manage face-threatening situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating responses to gaffes, identify which remedial moves are attempted and whether humour serves to repair or further expose the actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary laughter as socialization and ridicule-teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter directed at others' embarrassment functions disciplinarily: it teaches the offender appropriate behaviour and also models for the child how to laugh at and ridicule others, thereby reproducing social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to interpret laughter as an instrument of social control and transmission: analyse who is being taught and what norms are reinforced by the laughter (Freud/Graf Little Hans example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial/self-deception about the cruelty of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers commonly claim they are 'just laughing' to mask the disciplinary or cruel aspects of their laughter; such denial hides the role of laughter in enforcing norms and in learning repression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying audience accounts or participants' explanations, treat claims of 'just joking' as potential self-deceptive rhetorical moves that may conceal normative enforcement.
